descripcion_es: Expressing probability, caution and degrees of certainty.
resumen: Ways to avoid making blunt statements: modal verbs, adverbs of probability and cautious expressions (hedging). Highly valued in presentations and academic writing.

explicacion.texto: In formal English, people avoid sounding categorical. Instead of “This policy is a failure”, “This policy appears to have largely failed” is preferred. Caution is expressed with modals, verbs such as seem/appear/tend, adverbs and quantifiers.

filas: Growth is likely to slow down.
The measure might not be enough.
Rates are unlikely to fall soon.
there is a good chance that
quite probable (es: hay muchas posibilidades de que)
There is a good chance that it will pass.
The policy appears to be working.
usually do, have a tendency to (es: tender a, soler)
it can be argued that (es: posiblemente, cabe sostener que)
It is arguably the best novel of the decade.
it is reasonable to suppose (es: es de suponer que)
according to what people say (es: al parecer, según parece)
to some extent / to a certain degree
partly, not completely (es: hasta cierto punto)
To some extent, that is true.
mostly / in general terms (es: en gran medida / en líneas generales)
a little, slightly (es: algo, un tanto)
It would seem that the data is incomplete.
one could argue (es: cabría argumentar que)
It could be argued that the tax is unfair.
according to my knowledge (es: que yo sepa)
As far as I know, nothing has changed.
usually / in general (es: en la mayoría de los casos / en general)
I tend to believe (es: me inclino a pensar que)
I'm inclined to think he's right.

items: Scale of certainty: certainly > probably > possibly > unlikely > certainly not.
Watch the word order: “will probably” but “probably won't”.
“Likely” is an adjective: “It is likely to rain” or “It will likely rain” (more American); not “It likely rains”.

ejemplos.frase: The new rules are likely to affect small businesses most.
ejemplos.traduccion: Es probable que las nuevas normas afecten sobre todo a las pequeñas empresas.

ejemplos.frase: Apparently, the restaurant is closing next month.
ejemplos.traduccion: Al parecer, el restaurante cierra el mes que viene.

ejemplos.frase: She is arguably the finest tennis player of her generation.
ejemplos.traduccion: Posiblemente sea la mejor tenista de su generación.

ejemplos.frase: To some extent, the crisis was predictable.
ejemplos.traduccion: Hasta cierto punto, la crisis era previsible.

ejemplos.frase: He probably won't come to the party.
ejemplos.traduccion: Probablemente no venga a la fiesta.

ejemplos.frase: The results seem to suggest a link between diet and mood.
ejemplos.traduccion: Los resultados parecen indicar una relación entre la dieta y el estado de ánimo.

errores_hispanohablantes.mal: It's probable that he comes tomorrow.
errores_hispanohablantes.nota: “will probably” or “is likely to” is preferred; after “it's probable that”, the present tense is not used with future meaning.

errores_hispanohablantes.mal: Eventually the meeting will be cancelled.
errores_hispanohablantes.nota: “Eventually” does not mean “possibly, perhaps” (Spanish “eventualmente”), but “in the end”.
Spanish “hasta cierto punto” is “to some extent”.

ejercicios.frase: Inflation is ___ to fall next year, according to most analysts.
ejercicios.explicacion: This uses the table structure “is likely to / will probably”, that is, be likely to + infinitive to say that something is probable. The clue is the combination “is ___ to fall”: between the verb be and the to-infinitive only an adjective that takes to can fit, and likely is exactly that kind of adjective. The result is “Inflation is likely to fall”, with the caution typical of a forecast based on analysts. Neither probably, possibly nor maybe can be followed by to + infinitive.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: The structure is “be likely to + infinitive”.
ejercicios.traduccion: Según la mayoría de los analistas, es probable que la inflación baje el año que viene.

por_opcion.likely: Correct. Likely is an adjective and forms the structure be likely to + infinitive: “it is probable that it will fall”.
por_opcion.probably: Incorrect. Probably is an adverb and does not take to; we would say “Inflation will probably fall”, with will and without to.
por_opcion.possibly: Incorrect. Possibly is an adverb and cannot go between is and to fall; you would have to say “Inflation will possibly fall”, which is unusual.
por_opcion.maybe: Incorrect. Maybe is an informal adverb that usually goes at the start of the sentence (“Maybe inflation will fall”), never between be and to.

ejercicios.frase: She won't probably accept the offer.
respuestas: She probably won't accept the offer.
She probably will not accept the offer.
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the key point from the card “Watch the word order: will probably but probably won't”. In affirmative sentences the adverb goes after the auxiliary (she will probably accept), but in negative sentences it goes before the contracted form won't. The clue is precisely won't: you cannot insert probably between will and not when they are contracted. The correction is “She probably won't accept the offer”; the uncontracted form “She probably will not accept the offer” is also acceptable.

errores_previstos.respuesta: She won't probably accept the offer.
errores_previstos.explicacion: This copies the sentence without correcting it: probably cannot go after won't; in negative sentences it goes before.

errores_previstos.respuesta: She will probably not to accept the offer.
errores_previstos.explicacion: After will the verb goes in the infinitive without to; also, the natural contraction is lost.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Probably she doesn't accept the offer.
errores_previstos.explicacion: It uses the present simple as if it were future, copying the Spanish subjunctive “no acepte”; English needs will or won't.

ejercicios.enunciado: Complete with one word (partly, not completely).
ejercicios.frase: To some ___, the critics are right.
ejercicios.explicacion: The table gives “to some extent / to a certain degree” as equivalents of Spanish “hasta cierto punto”. The clue is the beginning “To some ___”, which only allows the noun of that fixed expression: extent or degree. With it the speaker partly agrees without fully accepting the criticism, a very useful nuance in debates. Both answers are valid because “to some extent” and “to some degree” are interchangeable.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: “To some extent / to some degree” = partly (es: hasta cierto punto).
ejercicios.traduccion: Hasta cierto punto, los críticos tienen razón.

errores_previstos.explicacion: “To some point” is a literal translation of Spanish “hasta cierto punto”; in English the expression is to some extent or to some degree.
“In some way” means “somehow, in a certain manner”, not “partly”; and “to some way” does not exist.
Extend is the verb (“make longer or wider”); the noun in the expression is extent, with a t.

ejercicios.frase: The new policy ___ to be working, but it is too early to say.
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the row “seem to / appear to” from the table: appear to + infinitive means “seem” with a cautious tone. The clue is “___ to be working” followed by “but it is too early to say”: the speaker does not want to state it with certainty, but to present it as an impression. That is why “The new policy appears to be working” is the right option: the verb appear in the third person plus to + continuous infinitive.
ejercicios.traduccion: La nueva política parece estar funcionando, pero es demasiado pronto para decirlo.

por_opcion.appears: Correct. Appear to + infinitive means “seem” and expresses exactly the caution that the second part of the sentence requires.
por_opcion.looks like: Incorrect. Look like is followed by a noun or a clause (“looks like it is working”), not by to + infinitive.
por_opcion.is bound: Incorrect. Be bound to expresses near certainty, the opposite of “it is too early to say”, and it would also make the sentence contradictory.
por_opcion.tends: Incorrect. Tend to talks about general tendencies or habits (“usually”), not about an impression of a specific situation.

ejercicios.frase: With so many delays, the project is ___ to go over budget.
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the row “will certainly / is bound to”, which puts be bound to at the top of the scale of certainty. The clue is “With so many delays”: the cause is so clear that the result is almost taken for granted, and the instruction explicitly asks for near certainty. The result is “the project is bound to go over budget”, with be bound to + infinitive. Unlikely would say the opposite, and apparent and arguable do not take to + infinitive.
ejercicios.traduccion: Con tantos retrasos, es casi seguro que el proyecto supere el presupuesto.

por_opcion.bound: Correct. Be bound to + infinitive means “it is certain that, it is destined to”, the near certainty the sentence requires.
por_opcion.unlikely: Incorrect. Be unlikely to means “it is improbable”, the opposite of what so many delays suggest.
por_opcion.apparent: Incorrect. Apparent means “evident, seeming” and is not used with to + infinitive; you would say “it is apparent that…”.
por_opcion.arguable: Incorrect. Arguable means “debatable, defensible” and does not take to + infinitive either; it is used in “it is arguable that…”.

glosario.significado: ser seguro que, estar abocado a

ejercicios.enunciado: Complete with an adverb (possibly, it can be argued).
ejercicios.frase: It is ___ the most important reform of the decade.
ejercicios.explicacion: The table defines arguably as “possibly, it can be argued that”. The clue is the superlative “the most important reform”: stating it without nuance would be blunt, and arguably presents it as an opinion that can be defended with arguments. It goes between is and the superlative, just as in the table example “It is arguably the best novel of the decade”. It is a very common adverb in analytical texts.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: “Arguably” = it can be argued that, possibly.
ejercicios.traduccion: Cabe sostener que es la reforma más importante de la década.

errores_previstos.explicacion: Eventually means “in the end, over time”, not “possibly”; it is the false friend that the card points out.
Arguable is the adjective; before a superlative you need the adverb arguably.
Probable is an adjective and cannot modify the superlative like this; it also lacks the “defensible opinion” nuance of arguably.

ejercicios.frase: Older people ___ to vote more than younger people.
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the row “tend to”, which translates Spanish “tender a, soler”. The clue is that the sentence describes the general behaviour of a group, not a certain fact in every case; tend to softens the generalisation. The result is “Older people tend to vote more”, with tend in the plural because the subject is people. The other options look similar but mean very different things.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: “Tend to” = usually do (es: tender a, soler).
ejercicios.traduccion: Las personas mayores suelen votar más que los jóvenes.

por_opcion.tend: Correct. Tend to + infinitive means “usually do, have a tendency to” and qualifies a generalisation about a group.
por_opcion.trend: Incorrect. Trend is a noun (“tendency, fashion”), not a verb that can be followed by to vote.
por_opcion.tense: Incorrect. Tense means “nervous, tight” (adjective) or “verb tense” (noun); it has nothing to do with “usually”.
por_opcion.intend: Incorrect. Intend to means “plan to, have the intention of”, which would change the meaning: the sentence is not about what they plan to do, but about what they usually do.

ejercicios.frase: Eventually it will rain this afternoon, so take an umbrella.
respuestas: It might rain this afternoon, so take an umbrella.
It may rain this afternoon, so take an umbrella.
It could rain this afternoon, so take an umbrella.
Possibly it will rain this afternoon, so take an umbrella.
ejercicios.explicacion: Among the typical mistakes, the card warns that eventually does not mean “possibly, perhaps” (Spanish “eventualmente”), but “in the end”. The clue is “so take an umbrella”: the sentence is about a possibility, not something that will happen sooner or later. For possibility the table gives may, might and could, so the correction is “It might / may / could rain this afternoon”. “Possibly it will rain” is also accepted, although it is less natural than the modals.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: “Eventually” means “in the end”; for possibility, use might/may/could.
ejercicios.traduccion: Puede que llueva esta tarde, así que coge un paraguas.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Eventually it will rain this afternoon, so take an umbrella.
errores_previstos.explicacion: This leaves the sentence uncorrected: eventually means “in the end” and does not express possibility.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Eventually it might rain this afternoon, so take an umbrella.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Changing the verb is not enough: eventually still means “in the end” and is unnecessary; the modal might already expresses possibility.

errores_previstos.respuesta: It will eventually rain this afternoon, so take an umbrella.
errores_previstos.explicacion: It only changes the word order; eventually is still the false friend and the sentence says that it will definitely rain in the end.

ejercicios.enunciado: Complete with an adverb (according to what people say).
ejercicios.explicacion: The table defines apparently as “according to what people say”. The clue is that the sentence reports news that the speaker has heard but not checked; the adverb at the start, followed by a comma, marks that distance. The result is “Apparently, the director resigned this morning”. Reportedly (“according to reports”) is also accepted; it is not in the table but has the same journalistic nuance of unconfirmed information.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: “Apparently” introduces something heard but not confirmed.
ejercicios.traduccion: Al parecer, el director dimitió esta mañana.

errores_previstos.explicacion: Apparent is an adjective (“evident”); to modify the whole sentence you need the adverb apparently.
Eventually means “in the end”, not “apparently”; it would change the meaning of the news.
Seemingly means “apparently” in the sense of “at first sight”, and it usually qualifies an adjective; to present hearsay news, apparently is the natural choice.

ejercicios.frase: The results were ___ disappointing, but not a disaster.
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the row “somewhat / rather”, which means “a little, slightly”. The clue is “but not a disaster”: the speaker reduces the intensity of the adjective disappointing. Somewhat is an adverb of degree that goes before the adjective and softens the criticism. The other options are words with some that do not work as intensifiers.
ejercicios.traduccion: Los resultados fueron algo decepcionantes, pero no un desastre.

por_opcion.somewhat: Correct. Somewhat means “a little, slightly” and modifies the adjective disappointing, softening it.
por_opcion.somehow: Incorrect. Somehow means “in some way, for some reason” and does not grade an adjective.
por_opcion.something: Incorrect. Something is a pronoun (“a thing”), not an adverb of degree; “something disappointing” would be “a disappointing thing”, used as a noun.
por_opcion.someway: Incorrect. Someway is a rare, colloquial form of “somehow” (“in some way”); it does not mean “slightly”.

ejercicios.frase: He will probably win the election.
respuestas: He is likely to win the election.
He is very likely to win the election.
ejercicios.explicacion: The card presents “is likely to / will probably” in the same row: they are two ways of expressing probability. The clue is the required beginning “He is”, which needs the adjective likely followed by to + infinitive. So will probably win becomes “He is likely to win the election”. “very likely” is also accepted; it strengthens the probability slightly without changing the structure.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: “Will probably” is equivalent to “be likely to”.
ejercicios.traduccion: Es probable que gane las elecciones.

errores_previstos.respuesta: He is likely to will win the election.
errores_previstos.explicacion: After to comes the infinitive without will: likely already conveys the idea of a probable future.

errores_previstos.respuesta: He is likely that he wins the election.
errores_previstos.explicacion: With a personal subject the structure is be likely to + infinitive; that is only used after “It is likely that…”.

errores_previstos.respuesta: He is probable to win the election.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Probable does not allow a personal subject with to + infinitive; that structure only works with likely.

ejercicios.enunciado: Complete with one word (according to my knowledge).
ejercicios.frase: As ___ as I know, the shop opens at nine.
ejercicios.explicacion: The table gives “as far as I know” as “according to my knowledge” (Spanish “que yo sepa”). The clue is the structure “As ___ as I know”: it is a fixed comparison with far, which limits the statement to what the speaker knows. In this way the information about the timetable is given cautiously, in case it has changed. No other word fits: “as long as” or “as much as” mean different things.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: “As far as I know” = according to my knowledge (es: que yo sepa).
ejercicios.traduccion: Que yo sepa, la tienda abre a las nueve.

errores_previstos.explicacion: “As much as I know” is not the fixed expression; English uses as far as I know.
“As long as” means “provided that, while”; it changes the meaning completely.
“As soon as” means “immediately when”; it does not express the limit of one's knowledge.

respuestas: It could be argued that the tax is unfair
ejercicios.explicacion: The table includes “it could be argued that”, translated as Spanish “cabría argumentar que”. It is an impersonal hedging expression: the empty subject It, the modal could, the passive be argued and the conjunction that, followed by the clause “the tax is unfair”. This construction lets you present a critical opinion without attributing it directly to the speaker, which is very useful in an oral exam on economic policy.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Impersonal hedging expression: “It could be argued that...”.
ejercicios.traduccion: Cabría argumentar que el impuesto es injusto.

errores_previstos.respuesta: It could be argued the tax that is unfair
errores_previstos.explicacion: That must go right after argued to introduce the full clause “the tax is unfair”.

errores_previstos.respuesta: It be could argued that the tax is unfair
errores_previstos.explicacion: The modal could goes before the infinitive be: could be argued.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Could be argued that the tax is unfair
errores_previstos.explicacion: A literal translation of Spanish “cabría argumentar”, without a subject; in English the subject It is obligatory, and a word is also missing.

ejercicios.frase: Interest rates are ___ to fall before the summer; the bank has ruled it out.
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the row “is unlikely to / probably won't”, which expresses low probability. The decisive clue is the second part: “the bank has ruled it out”, that is, the bank has excluded it. Therefore the cut is improbable and the sentence is “Interest rates are unlikely to fall”. Likely, bound and sure would express probability or certainty, contradicting the fact that it has been ruled out.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: If the bank has ruled it out, it is improbable: “unlikely”.
ejercicios.traduccion: Es poco probable que los tipos de interés bajen antes del verano; el banco lo ha descartado.

por_opcion.unlikely: Correct. Be unlikely to means “it is improbable that”, consistent with the bank having ruled it out.
por_opcion.likely: Incorrect. Be likely to means “it is probable that”, which contradicts “the bank has ruled it out”.
por_opcion.bound: Incorrect. Be bound to expresses near certainty, which contradicts the ruling-out even more.
por_opcion.sure: Incorrect. Be sure to means “it is certain that”; it expresses certainty, not improbability.

ejercicios.enunciado: Complete with an adverb (mostly, to a great extent).
ejercicios.frase: The campaign was ___ successful, despite a few problems.
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the row “largely / broadly”, which means “mostly / in general terms”. The clue is “despite a few problems”: the success is not total, so the adverb limits its scope. Largely goes before the adjective successful. Broadly, from the same row, and mostly (“for the most part”) are also valid, with the same softening effect.
ejercicios.traduccion: La campaña tuvo éxito en gran medida, a pesar de algunos problemas.

errores_previstos.explicacion: Large is an adjective (“big”); before successful you need the adverb largely.
Greatly means “enormously” and intensifies instead of qualifying; it also does not combine naturally with successful.
Widely means “extensively, by many people” (widely known); it does not express “to a great extent” with successful.

descripcion_larga_es: Hedging means expressing an idea without stating it bluntly: with modals such as may or might, verbs such as seem, appear or tend, adverbs such as arguably or apparently, and quantifiers such as largely or to some extent. It is essential in oral presentations and in academic or economic writing, where sounding categorical reduces credibility. Spanish speakers find it difficult because they copy Spanish “eventualmente” or “es probable que” and put probably in the wrong place.

contexto.que_es: It is the set of devices that grade the certainty of a statement: from near certainty (be bound to, will certainly) to improbability (be unlikely to, probably won't). It includes softening verbs (seem, appear, tend), adverbs of cautious opinion (arguably, presumably, apparently) and words that limit the scope (largely, somewhat, to some extent).
contexto.por_que_importa: In formal English, a statement without nuance sounds arrogant or lacking in rigour, and an examiner notices it immediately. Knowing how to hedge lets you present data and opinions with the caution expected in a technical report or an oral presentation. Getting it wrong also causes confusion: someone who says “eventually” meaning “perhaps” is announcing that something will definitely happen in the end.
contexto.cuando_se_usa: It appears when presenting forecasts (inflation is likely to fall), results (the plan was largely successful), debatable opinions (it could be argued that…) or unconfirmed information (apparently, reportedly). Spanish speakers tend to say “It's probable that…” or “In some way…”, literal translations that sound unnatural; English prefers be likely to, to some extent and well-placed adverbs.
